newsitem.title: USA: Stocks fall on profit warnings, bonds up on inflation news.
newsitem.headline: Stocks fall on profit warnings, bonds up on inflation news.

text.p: Stocks fell on Wednesday amid warnings of disappointing profits by technology companies, while bonds rose on fresh news that inflation remains under control.
The dollar rebounded from early selling sparked by news of a sharp gain in Japan's trade surplus in May.
Oil prices fell sharply under pressure from excess supplies of crude and fast-growing refined product supply.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 42.07 points at 7,718.71, its third straight session of losses. In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,294 to 1,192 on moderate volume of 492 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Warnings by personal computer manufacturer Gateway 2000 Inc. that its second-quarter revenues would be about even with the first quarter and computer disk drive maker Seagate Technology Inc. of disappointing quarterly revenues raised concerns that trouble might lie ahead for the technology sector.
The earnings warnings sparked concern that the entire sector, which has run up during the past month, and possibly the broader market might suffer.
"There's been some suspicion that if there's no inflation ahead, we might have a slowdown, which would hurt earnings generally," said Harry Laubscher, an analyst at Tucker Anthony.

Some analysts waved off the earnings warnings, saying the sell-off was a knee-jerk reaction, noting that in the weeks leading up to the earnings reporting season, the stock market is often rocked by cautionary statements from companies.
"We are telling people to be very very cautious. Start taking some profits and buy bonds for safety," Laubscher said.

Gary Loe, an analyst for Anderson & Loe, a firm that advises money managers, said, "Some consolidation in stocks is certainly reasonable after the gains we've had. But my sense is we're in a very volatile period."
That volatility is expected to get stronger through the week as Friday's "triple witching" expiration of options and futures nears.
The dollar recovered after dipping under 113 yen on news that Japan's trade surplus swelled 222 percent to 738 billion yen ($6.53 billion) in May from a year earlier.
The dollar rose to 113.65 yen from 113.32 yen late Tuesday. It also sprang back from an overnight low of 1.7225 German marks to 1.7333 marks, vs. 1.7305 Tuesday.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted at $338.90/40, not far from the four-year low around $336.15 seen Feb. 15.
At New York's Commodity Exchange (COMEX), gold for August delivery ended down $2.80 at $341.00 an ounce, after seeing a new life-of-contract low at $340.60.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude for July delivery finished 44 cents off at $18.79 a barrel while July gasoline settled a steep 1.70 cents off at 56.78 cents a gallon. July heating oil ended 1.01 cents a gallon lower at 51.44 cents.

Soybean futures also tumbled on the Chicago Board of Trade as fund managers liquidated their long positions in the July contract following its recent extreme volatility. Soybeans for July delivery ended 20-1/2 cents lower at $8.32-1/2 a bushel.
Overseas, London's FTSE index index closed 25.2 points lower at 4,657. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,497.85, down 95.81 points, or 0.47 percent.
